stances.claim: This is the wrong time for Cha-cha -- the public is so wary of past attempts that the topic itself 'turns them off completely.'

The Constitution is imperfect (verbose, vague, awkwardly phrased) and certain provisions deserve revisiting -- national territory, party-list, foreign restrictions on natural resources -- but only 'at the right time, in the right way, for the right reasons, and by the right persons/entities.'
No revision of the Charter is historically possible without presidential backing -- every successful change has had the incumbent president's intervention and support.

President Bongbong Marcos has shown no interest in Cha-cha -- not in his pre-election speeches or in his July SONA -- so without his enthusiastic support 'no constitutional revision is possible' and any further discussion would be 'useless divisionary chatter.'

The right answer to joblessness, high prices, and agonizing poverty is not Cha-cha but changing the officials who subvert our institutions -- both a change of leaders and a change in our leaders, 'from the inside out, a change of hearts, a change of values.'

one_paragraph_summary: Invited by Rep. Rufus B. Rodriguez (chair of the House committee on constitutional amendments) to a Jan. 26 public hearing 'consulting' him on the necessity, mode, and substance of Charter change, Panganiban -- citing schedule and doctor's advice -- declines personally and answers in writing. He believes this is 'not the right time' for Cha-cha: the public has grown so wary of past attempts that the very mention turns them off. He concedes the 1987 Constitution is imperfect -- verbose, vague, awkwardly phrased, with provisions on national territory, the party-list system, and foreign restrictions on natural resources that deserve revisiting 'at the right time, in the right way, for the right reasons, and by the right persons/entities.' He reminds readers that no Charter in the world is perfect (the US Constitution, oldest at September 17, 1787, ratified June 21, 1788, amended 27 times, still permits Electoral-College results where Bush and Trump won despite fewer popular votes than Gore and Clinton), and that historically no revision succeeds without presidential backing -- from Quezon and Roxas (1935 amendments) to Marcos Sr. (1973 Constitution) and Cory Aquino (1987 Constitution). Subsequent attempts have failed: Ramos and Arroyo's people's-initiative drives were struck down in Santiago v. Comelec (March 19, 1997) and Lambino v. Comelec (Oct. 25, 2006); Estrada's Preparatory Commission on Constitutional Reforms under CJ Andres R. Narvasa was overtaken by his Edsa II ouster; and Duterte's Consultative Commission under CJ Reynato S. Puno drafted a sweeping 'Bayanihan Constitution' that went nowhere in Congress. President Bongbong Marcos has shown no interest in Cha-cha -- not in his pre-election speeches, not in his July SONA -- so without his enthusiastic support 'no constitutional revision is possible' and further discussion would be 'useless divisionary chatter.' The right answer to joblessness, high prices, and agonizing poverty is not Cha-cha but 'changing the officials who subvert our institutions' -- both a change of leaders and a change in our leaders, 'from the inside out, a change of hearts, a change of values.' He closes with the antinomic civic-virtue catalogue: more patriotism, less formalism; more delicadeza, less legalism; more substance, less rhetoric; more action, less talk; more dedication to duty, less posturing; more economics, less politics; more truth, less duplicity; more ethics, less image-building; more integrity, less bigotry.
